summary: The day lends itself to two SQL tasks that run on sqlite3 in memory, a finding query for duplicates on a business key and a LAG window over each ticket's events; its warehousing, architecture, vendor, BigQuery-loading and nesting steps are concepts, cloud tools or GoogleSQL that SQLite lacks, and the extract's two file writers are demo 01's rung.

steps.title: What a data warehouse is, and OLTP against OLAP
steps.reason: The step teaches concepts (what a warehouse is, OLTP against OLAP, row against column storage), and its two queries are week 3's lookup and GROUP BY used as illustrations. A task here would practise week 3's SQL, not the step's point, and a check cannot see why a workload is OLAP.

steps.title: Warehouse architecture, data lakes, the ODS and data marts
steps.reason: Layers, lakes against warehouses, the ODS and dependent or independent marts are concepts with no code on the page; the only wrong answer a check could see is not writing anything.

steps.title: Data store vendors: cloud against on-premises
steps.reason: Vendor names, cost, scaling and maintenance trade-offs and serverless are concepts for an interview answer; nothing on the page runs, so there is no behaviour to check.

steps.title: Data quality problems and cleansing
steps.reason: The finding queries (NOT IN, GROUP BY on a business key with HAVING, a join comparing timestamps) run unchanged on sqlite3 in memory and return rows a check reads, and the page names the surrogate-key mistake (event_id differs between copies). Demo 02's explore.sql takes the three event queries, so the task is a sibling on customers: duplicates on email as the business key, found and never removed (removal is Thursday's).

steps.title: Extracting a transactional database into files
steps.reason: The checkable behaviour here, a CSV with a header and empty fields for None and one JSON object per line with default=str, is exactly demo 01's write_csv and write_jsonl, the second with its own test, so any task would hand over the rung. The rest (parents before children, .gitignore, files before loads) is convention.

steps.title: BigQuery: architecture, datasets, tables and loads
steps.reason: Datasets, bq mk, bq load, schema files, ALTER TABLE options and IAM shares need BigQuery and the bq tool, neither of which the runtime has; rebuilding a schema list or a seconds conversion in Python would practise a stand-in, not the step.

steps.title: BigQuery queries and advanced queries
steps.reason: Window functions (ROW_NUMBER, LAG with PARTITION BY and ORDER BY) and WITH RECURSIVE run on SQLite 3.39.0, and the page names the mistake a check catches: GROUP BY collapses rows where a window keeps them. QUALIFY and DATETIME_DIFF are not in SQLite, so the task avoids both; setup can ATTACH an in-memory database as desk_raw so desk_raw.ticket_events runs unchanged. Demo 02 takes LAG(created_at), so the task reads LAG(kind).

steps.title: Denormalisation and nested fields
steps.reason: The step's code is ARRAY_AGG(STRUCT(...)), which SQLite does not have; json_group_array would fake it. Without nesting, the wide board join is week 3's JOIN, and the trade-off itself is a concept.

tasks.title: Data quality
tasks.idea: The reader writes one finding query over customers (customer_id, name, email, country, monthly_fee) that lists each email held by more than one customer row, with columns email and copies, ordered by email. With two rows for ana@example.com and one each for the others, it returns one row: ana@example.com, 2. It finds the duplicates and removes nothing.
checks: The duplicated email comes back with copies 2; grouping on customer_id, the surrogate key that differs between the two copies, returns no rows.
An email held by one customer row does not appear; leaving out HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 returns every email.

The result columns are email and copies in that order, and the customers table still holds every row afterwards; a DELETE of the extra copy, removal the page leaves to a later step, changes the count.

tasks.title: GoogleSQL
tasks.idea: The reader writes one query over desk_raw.ticket_events (event_id, ticket_id, kind, note, created_at) returning event_id, ticket_id, kind and previous_kind, where previous_kind is LAG(kind) OVER (PARTITION BY ticket_id ORDER BY event_id), ordered by event_id. On ticket 4 (open, assigned, assigned) it gives NULL, open, assigned.
checks: Every event comes back as its own row, one per event; GROUP BY ticket_id collapses each ticket to one row.
The first event of each ticket has previous_kind NULL; leaving out PARTITION BY gives it the last kind of the ticket before.
Inside a ticket, previous_kind is the kind of the event with the next lower event_id; ordering the window by kind instead gives a different previous_kind.
